name: Warrior I
hero_alt: Warrior I, seen from the side
meta_description: Back heel lifting, back knee bending, hips twisting open, torso leaning? Five things usually hold back Warrior I, and a daily exercise that fixes each one.
og_description: Five things usually hold back Warrior I, and a daily exercise that fixes each one.
lede: Front knee over the ankle at a right angle, back heel down, hips facing forward, arms reaching straight up. Here’s the rubric Posewise measures it against, and what to train when you miss.
rubric_intro: Posewise checks nine things, from the side and the front. Here’s what good looks like.

rubric.name: Front knee
rubric.good: Bent to a right angle, over the ankle

rubric.name: Knee tracking
rubric.good: Over your front foot, not caving in

rubric.name: Arms
rubric.good: Straight up, in line with your ears

rubric.name: Shoulders
rubric.good: Level, both arms at the same height

fixes.outcome: your front knee will reach a 90° bend.
fixes.why: The shape is there, the depth isn’t. That usually points to leg strength, not technique.
fixes.cue: Bend your front knee toward 90°, right over your ankle.

fixes.outcome: your back heel will stay down and your back leg will straighten.
fixes.why: With the back heel grounded, tight calves usually lift the heel or pull the back knee into a bend. Shorten your stance until they ease.
fixes.cue: Press your back heel down into the mat.

fixes.outcome: your torso will stay tall and your hips will turn toward the front.
fixes.why: Tight hip flexors on the back leg tip the pelvis forward and pull that hip open, so the chest leans and the hips twist.
fixes.cue: Draw your back hip forward and lift your chest.

fixes.outcome: your front knee will track over your toes.
fixes.why: When the outer glutes are weak, the front knee caves in toward the big toe.
fixes.cue: Track your front knee out over your middle toe.

fixes.outcome: your arms will reach straight up, in line with your ears.
fixes.why: When shoulder range runs out overhead, the arms angle forward, one side rides higher, or the shoulders creep toward the ears.
fixes.cue: Reach your arms up in line with your ears, through your fingertips.

faq.q: Should my back heel be down in Warrior I?
faq.a: Yes. Turn your back foot out about 45° and press the heel into the mat. If it won’t stay down, shorten your stance; a lifted heel turns the pose into Crescent Lunge.

faq.q: Do my hips need to be square in Warrior I?
faq.a: Point them forward as far as is comfortable, but most bodies can’t fully square them with the back heel down. Stepping your feet a little wider apart, hip-width rather than heel to heel, helps.

faq.q: Why does my lower back hurt in Warrior I?
faq.a: Usually tight hip flexors on the back leg tip the pelvis forward and arch the low back. Shorten your stance and draw your tailbone down as you lift your chest.

faq.q: What’s the difference between Warrior I and Warrior II?
faq.a: Warrior I faces the front with your arms overhead. Warrior II opens your hips and chest to the side with your arms out at shoulder height.

faq.q: How can I check my Warrior I form at home?
faq.a: Film yourself from the side and the front. Or use Posewise, an iPhone app that measures your Warrior I with the camera, speaks corrections as you hold it, and builds a six-minute daily plan for what it finds.

llms_summary: the five things that usually hold back Warrior I (leg strength for a 90° front knee, tight calves lifting the back heel and bending the back leg, tight hip flexors tipping the torso and twisting the hips, outer-hip strength for knee tracking, shoulder mobility for arms overhead), with the alignment rubric and a daily exercise for each.
